lines.cap: **Narrator:** Monday. Room 8H. Mr Hargreaves is on mug number seventeen, and Mei is clutching her phone.
**Mr H:** Timed essay: '**Mobile phones should be banned in schools.**' **Discuss**.
**Mei:** Line one: 'I THINK BANNING PHONES IS STUPID AND ANYONE WHO AGREES IS CLUELESS, EXCLAMATION MARK!'
**Nib:** ALL CAPS?! Five exclamation marks?! I have leaked straight through the desk!
**One Hand:** Steady now. On the **one hand**, phones distract pupils and can fuel lunchtime cyberbullying.
**Other Hand:** **On the other hand**, phones are pocket dictionaries and keep parents in touch on the MRT!
**Mei:** Why are two giant velvet gloves sitting on Mr H's desk?!
**Will:** In my plays, two sides settle an argument with rapiers! Though brass scales are shinier.
**Mei:** Arguing fairly with people who want my phone: **one star**.
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode twelve: On the Other Hand.
**Narrator:** Tuesday. The brass scales have claimed the front desk.
**Nib:** **Discursive** comes from Latin *discurrere*, '**to run to and fro**' — like Montaigne's *essayer*, 'to try' an idea.
**Mr H:** Know the spectrum. **Persuasive** writing pushes **one** view using emotive language and rhetorical questions.
**Mr H:** **Argumentative** writing also picks **one** side from paragraph one, defending it with logic.
**One Hand:** **Discursive** writing explores **both sides fairly** in a calm tone, holding your verdict until the **conclusion**.
**Other Hand:** Spot the task command words: '**Discuss**', '**Consider both sides**', or '**To what extent**'!
**Mr H:** Fairness test: if a reader who **disagrees** with you finishes your essay and thinks, 'that was fair to my side', you've nailed it.
**Mr H:** Open with **CID**: **Context** why it matters now, **Issue** naming both sides, **Direction** signposting the weighing.
**Nib:** And like a detective in the CID, keep your **final verdict secret** in the introduction!
**Mei:** So I cut 'In this essay I will talk about', dictionary definitions, and 'Since the dawn of time'?
**Other Hand:** Instead, contrast both views vividly: some see zoos as modern **arks**, others as **prisons** with a gift shop!
**Narrator:** Wednesday. The library. Mei has forty-five minutes and zero plan.
**Mr H:** Never start writing at minute zero. Spend **five to eight minutes** on a **T-chart** plan: For and Against.
**One Hand:** Star the **best three** points on each side, and decide your **final judgement** before you write line one.
**Mr H:** Way one: **block structure**. All arguments **for**, a turning-point sentence, then all arguments **against**. Safe and clear.
**Other Hand:** Way two: **alternating structure** — point and counterpoint clash **inside each paragraph** by aspect, like cost or wellbeing!
**Mei:** Like on a four-day school week: paragraph one weighs rested pupils against tired eight-year-olds; paragraph two weighs school bills against childcare!
**One Hand:** And remember: **balance** means treating both sides **fairly**, not counting out the exact same number of words!
**Nib:** Top-band secret: whichever structure you choose, put the side you finally **agree with second**.
**Mei:** Aha! Because the side the reader hears **last** leads straight into my conclusion! Two stars!
**Mr H:** Write for thirty minutes, and save **five minutes** at the end to check markers and punctuation.
**Narrator:** Thursday. Room 8H. Nib is patrolling Mei's essay with a magnifying glass.
**Nib:** Discursive essays demand a **formal register**: no slang like 'loads of kids', no contractions, no loaded insults like '**ridiculous**'!
**One Hand:** Use **impersonal constructions** and the **passive voice** to stay objective: '**It could be argued that**...', '**It has been suggested that**...'
**Other Hand:** And pick exact **reporting verbs**: critics **suggest**, campaigners **insist**, supporters **concede**!
**Mr H:** Climb only as high up the certainty ladder as your proof allows. **Could, may, might: keep your claims light**.
**Mei:** Not 'All teenagers are addicted to phones' — '**Many** teenagers report they **may** find it hard to switch off'! Though don't over-hedge into mush!
**Nib:** Signpost every turn with **discourse markers**: **furthermore** to add, **conversely** for the opposite side, **nevertheless** for 'despite that', **consequently** for a result!
**Mei:** Look! 'Phones can distract pupils, **however**, they help with research.' Done!
**Kevin:** COMMA SPLICE! You joined two complete sentences with just ME before 'however'! I can't hold two whole clauses! Get the bag!
**Mr H:** When '**however**' joins two full sentences, put a **semicolon before** it and a **comma after** it.
**Kevin:** Semicolon in front, Kevin right after 'however,'! Oh, look at us! Punctuation teamwork!
**Narrator:** Thursday afternoon. Debate stage in the school hall.
**Mr H:** Four kinds of **evidence**, strongest to weakest: **large studies**, **expert opinion**, **real-world examples**, and a lone **anecdote**.
**One Hand:** Real example: captive breeding saved the **Arabian oryx** after it went extinct in the wild!
**Mr H:** Never invent fake statistics and pin them on a real organisation. In practice essays, label them '**hypothetical**' — 'Imagine a survey...'
**Other Hand:** And interrogate the other side's evidence! Who funded that uniform survey — a company that **sells school uniforms**?!
**Will:** To crush my opponents, I shall claim homework-haters despise all human knowledge! Behold my scarecrow!
**Other Hand:** That's a **straw man**, Will — exaggerating the other side so it's easy to knock over! Present their **strongest** case: **steelmanning**!
**Nib:** Then answer with a **rebuttal** using the concede-then-counter engine: '**Admittedly... However... Therefore...**'
**Mei:** Let's build a **PEER** paragraph — PEEL with a **Reply**! **Point**: Supporters of a phone ban argue notifications fracture concentration.
**Mei:** **Evidence**: Teachers report pupils can take several minutes to refocus after a single buzz.
**Mei:** **Explain**: **This suggests that** phones quietly erode lesson time, even when nobody is texting.
**Mei:** **Reply**: **Admittedly**, phones aid quick research; **however**, school laptops provide that benefit without personal group chats.
**One Hand:** The scales just tipped! Three and a half stars!

chapters.title: Weigh it, judge it, finish it

lines.cap: **Narrator:** Friday. Mei reaches her final paragraph.
**Mei:** Conclusion: 'There are good points on both sides, so it's up to the reader to decide!'
**Mr H:** Off the fence, Mei. '**Discuss**' still requires a reasoned verdict. Use **WJF**: **Weigh, Judge, Finish**.
**One Hand:** **Weigh** the strongest point on each side, **Judge** starting with '**On balance...**', and **Finish** with a final thought — **zero new arguments**!
**Other Hand:** Even smarter is a **qualified judgement** — 'yes, **provided that**...': lock phones away in lessons, allow them on the journey home!
**Nib:** Or on school uniform: 'A uniform should make pupils **equal, not identical**.' Crisp!
**Mr H:** In Term 3, you'll also write discursive essays on the **novel**: 'Is Scrooge's change in A Christmas Carol **believable**?'
**Other Hand:** Against: nobody reverses a lifetime of greed in **one night** just from a fright!
**One Hand:** For: Dickens plants the lonely schoolboy in Stave Two and that '**solitary as an oyster**' pearl — plus it's a **moral fable**, not realism!
**Mei:** **On balance**, the speed strains realism, yet within Dickens's ghostly fable the transformation feels earned!
**Mr H:** Balanced, hedged, and judged. I might even let you keep your phone at break.
**Narrator:** Before pens down, the scales of Room 8H would like to save you some marks.
**Mei:** Memory hooks! **CID** for the intro — keep the verdict secret; **PEER** to add a Reply in body paragraphs!
**One Hand:** **Could, may, might: keep your claims light**; and **WJF** — **Weigh, Judge, Finish** — in the conclusion!
**Mr H:** One. Never blurt your **final opinion** in the introduction — save it for the conclusion.
**Nib:** Two. Don't write a one-sided **persuasive rant** or use slang and loaded words like 'stupid' or 'clueless'.
**Other Hand:** Three. Don't **sit on the fence** at the end, and never drop a **brand-new argument** into the conclusion!
**Will:** Four. Never set up a weak **straw man**, and never fake real statistics — label practice ones **hypothetical**!
**Mr H:** Five. Always **explain** your evidence with 'This suggests that...' — never drop and run.
**Kevin:** Six. Joining two full sentences with '**however**'? **Semicolon before, comma after**! Save a comma's life!
**Mei:** **On balance**, discursive writing gets **four and a half stars** — provided nobody takes my phone on the MRT.
**Will:** Admittedly, she withheld half a star; nevertheless, her hedging was impeccable.
**Mr H:** Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** What do the three letters of **CID** stand for in a discursive introduction?
**Mei:** **Context, Issue, and Direction** — keeping your final verdict secret!
**Mr H:** How do you punctuate '**however**' when it joins two complete sentences?
**Kevin:** A **semicolon before** 'however' and a **comma after** it!
**Mr H:** What do we call a weak, exaggerated version of the opposing view set up just to knock down?
**Other Hand:** A **straw man** argument! Present their strongest case instead.
**Mr H:** Which three discourse markers power the **concede-then-counter** rebuttal pattern?
**Nib:** '**Admittedly... However... Therefore...**'
**Mr H:** What three things must a discursive conclusion do: **WJF**?
**One Hand:** **Weigh** the strongest points, **Judge** with a reason, and **Finish** with a final thought!
**Mr H:** Brilliant work. Now try the **Discursive Writing** quiz in your English Lab.
**One Hand:** After you, Other Hand.
**Other Hand:** Conversely, after YOU, One Hand!
**Mr H:** You're going to be in that doorway until June.
